subject: combined-science

items.q: A gland of the endocrine system secretes a hormone. How does that hormone reach the organ where it produces an effect, and how do its effects compare with those of the nervous system?
items.correct: carried in the bloodstream; effects are slower but last longer
items.misconception: carried along nerves; effects are slower but last longer
items.why: Hormonal and nervous coordination are taught together, and both are described as ways of sending information around the body, so students merge the two and give hormones the pathway that belongs to nerve impulses. The endocrine system is composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream; the blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.
items.random_wrong: carried in the blood; effects are faster but end much sooner

items.q: A student labels endocrine glands on a diagram of the human body. Which label has been placed in the correct position?
items.correct: the thyroid gland labelled in the neck
items.misconception: the adrenal gland labelled inside the brain
items.why: The glands are learned as a list of names and functions rather than as positions on a diagram, so when a diagram is labelled students guess and swap glands that they have never located. Students should be able to identify the position of the pituitary gland, pancreas, thyroid, adrenal gland, ovary and testes on a diagram of the human body.
items.random_wrong: the pituitary gland labelled below the stomach

items.q: Why is the pituitary gland described as a 'master gland'?
items.correct: its hormones make other glands release hormones
items.misconception: its hormones produce all the body effects directly
items.why: The label 'master gland' suggests a gland that does everything itself, so students picture the pituitary acting straight on the body rather than acting through the glands it controls. The pituitary gland secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions, and these hormones in turn act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.
items.random_wrong: its hormones travel to the glands along nerves

items.q: After a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person who does not have diabetes rises above the normal level. What happens next?
items.correct: insulin is released and glucose enters the cells
items.misconception: insulin is released and glycogen forms in the blood
items.why: Students remember the pair of words 'glucose to glycogen' but not the step before it, so they leave the glucose in the blood where the hormone met it instead of moving it into cells first. Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells; in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
items.random_wrong: insulin is released so that glucose leaves the cells

items.q: A person's blood glucose concentration is too high. What happens to the excess glucose?
items.correct: it moves into cells and is stored as glycogen
items.misconception: it is changed into glycogen in the blood
items.why: Students remember the pair of words 'glucose to glycogen' but not the step before it, so they leave the glucose in the blood where the hormone met it instead of moving it into cells first. Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells; in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
items.random_wrong: it is released from the cells into the blood

items.q: What causes Type 1 diabetes?
items.correct: the pancreas fails to produce enough insulin
items.misconception: the body cells stop responding to insulin
items.why: Both types of diabetes are described as uncontrolled blood glucose, so students give them the same cause and apply the failure of the pancreas, which they met first in Type 1, to both. In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; it is Type 1 diabetes in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin.
items.random_wrong: the pancreas releases insulin when glucose is low

items.q: A person with Type 2 diabetes has a normal concentration of insulin in the blood but a high blood glucose concentration. Why?
items.correct: their body cells no longer respond to insulin
items.misconception: their pancreas has completely stopped making insulin
items.why: Both types of diabetes are described as uncontrolled blood glucose, so students give them the same cause and apply the failure of the pancreas, which they met first in Type 1, to both. In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; it is Type 1 diabetes in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin.
items.random_wrong: their insulin cannot act on glucose in the blood

items.q: A graph shows blood glucose concentration for two hours after a glucose drink. For a person without diabetes the concentration rises to a peak and then returns to its starting level. For a person with untreated Type 1 diabetes it rises higher and stays high. What does the graph show about the person with Type 1 diabetes?
items.correct: not enough insulin is produced to lower blood glucose
items.misconception: their body cells have stopped responding to insulin
items.why: Both types of diabetes are described as uncontrolled blood glucose, so students give them the same cause and apply the failure of the pancreas, which they met first in Type 1, to both. In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; it is Type 1 diabetes in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin.
items.random_wrong: their insulin cannot change glucose to glycogen

items.q: Several hours after a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person falls below the normal level. Which change restores it?
items.correct: glucagon is released and glycogen changes to glucose
items.misconception: insulin is released and stored glycogen changes to glucose
items.why: The words glucagon, glycogen and glucose look and sound almost the same, so students treat them as one idea and give glucagon the job of the hormone they met first. If the blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas produces the hormone glucagon that causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.
items.random_wrong: glucagon is released and the glucose changes to glycogen

items.q: What is the role of follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) in the menstrual cycle?
items.correct: it causes an egg to mature in the ovary
items.misconception: it causes a mature egg to be released
items.why: Both hormones come from the same gland, act on the same organ and are learned as a pair of initials, so the two jobs are easily swapped when the names are not linked to their meanings. Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary; luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg.
items.random_wrong: it keeps the lining of the uterus in place

items.q: Which interaction between hormones helps to control the menstrual cycle?
items.correct: oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH release
items.misconception: LH inhibits FSH and causes an egg to mature
items.why: Both hormones come from the same gland, act on the same organ and are learned as a pair of initials, so the two jobs are easily swapped when the names are not linked to their meanings. Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary; luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg.
items.random_wrong: FSH inhibits oestrogen and maintains the lining

items.q: A graph of hormone levels during the menstrual cycle shows the level of LH rising to a sharp peak on day 14. What is happening on day 14?
items.correct: an egg is being released from the ovary
items.misconception: an egg is starting to mature in the ovary
items.why: Both hormones come from the same gland, act on the same organ and are learned as a pair of initials, so the two jobs are easily swapped when the names are not linked to their meanings. Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary; luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg.
items.random_wrong: the lining of the uterus is being maintained

items.q: A woman wants a method of contraception that does not use hormones. Which method and reason are correct?
items.correct: a diaphragm, which stops sperm reaching eggs
items.misconception: a condom, which releases a hormone slowly
items.why: The methods are listed together under contraception and the hormonal ones are studied in most detail, so students carry the hormone explanation across to the methods that are purely physical. Barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms prevent the sperm reaching an egg; only the hormonal methods, such as oral contraceptives and slow release progesterone, work by altering hormone levels.
items.random_wrong: the pill, which kills sperm before they arrive

items.q: How do oral contraceptives that contain hormones prevent pregnancy?
items.correct: they inhibit FSH production so no eggs mature
items.misconception: they kill or disable sperm before fertilisation
items.why: All contraceptives are met as one list with one purpose, so students give them one shared mechanism, and stopping the sperm is the most obvious way to prevent fertilisation. Oral contraceptives contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature; it is spermicidal agents that kill or disable sperm.
items.random_wrong: they inhibit FSH so the uterus lining breaks down

items.q: A woman does not release eggs because her level of FSH is too low. Which treatment could allow her to become pregnant in the normal way?
items.correct: a fertility drug that contains FSH and LH
items.misconception: a fertility drug that contains progesterone
items.why: Four hormones are learned at once in one cycle, and students separate them into the pair with initials and the pair with names rather than by what each one does, so the two roles are exchanged. FSH causes maturation of an egg in the ovary and LH stimulates the release of the egg; oestrogen and progesterone are involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
items.random_wrong: IVF, in which eggs are fertilised in her body

items.q: Which statement about IVF treatment is correct?
items.correct: eggs are fertilised by sperm in the laboratory
items.misconception: eggs are fertilised by the sperm inside the mother
items.why: Fertility treatment is met as one idea, and because a fertility drug does lead to a pregnancy in the normal way, students assume IVF works the same way and miss the step outside the body that the name refers to. IVF involves giving a mother FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs; the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory, and at the stage when the fertilised eggs are tiny balls of cells one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus.
items.random_wrong: most IVF treatments result in a successful birth

items.q: A student is suddenly frightened by a loud noise. Which gland releases adrenaline, and what effect does it have?
items.correct: the adrenal gland; it speeds up the heart rate
items.misconception: the pituitary gland; it speeds up the heart rate
items.why: The pituitary is remembered as the gland that responds to body conditions and controls other glands, so students make it the source of the hormone released in an emergency instead of naming the gland it is called after. Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for 'flight or fight'.
items.random_wrong: the thyroid gland; it reduces the heart rate

items.q: The concentration of thyroxine in the blood of a person rises above the normal level. What happens next?
items.correct: thyroxine release is inhibited and the level falls
items.misconception: more thyroxine is released and the level rises
items.why: Students read feedback as the body responding to a rise by doing more of the same, and the word negative is taken to describe the hormone or the situation rather than the reversing of the change. Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback: a level above normal inhibits the release of thyroxine so that the level returns to normal, in the same way that insulin and glucagon return blood glucose concentration to normal.
items.random_wrong: the metabolic rate falls and the level stays high

items.q: Which statement about the main reproductive hormones is correct?
items.correct: testosterone is produced by the testes
items.misconception: oestrogen is produced by the pituitary gland
items.why: Students learn that the pituitary controls reproduction and that it is the master gland, and they take control of a process to mean production of every hormone involved in it. Oestrogen is the main female reproductive hormone produced in the ovary; testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone produced by the testes.
items.random_wrong: oestrogen is produced by the thyroid gland

items.q: A hormone is carried in the blood to every part of the body. Does it produce an effect everywhere?
items.correct: No. Although the blood carries it everywhere, the hormone produces its effect at a target organ.
items.misconception: A hormone produces an effect in every organ that the blood carries it to.
items.why: Students correctly learn that the blood reaches all organs, and then assume that anything carried in the blood must act on all of them, overlooking the idea of a target organ. The blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do the effects of the endocrine system compare with those of the nervous system?
items.correct: Compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.
items.misconception: Hormones act faster than nerve impulses and their effects wear off more quickly.
items.why: Adrenaline is often the first hormone students meet and it appears to act instantly in a frightening situation, so they generalise from it and reverse the comparison the specification makes. Compared to the nervous system the effects of the endocrine system are slower but act for longer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When does the pancreas produce insulin?
items.correct: The pancreas produces insulin if the blood glucose concentration is too high.
items.misconception: Insulin is produced when the blood glucose concentration is too low, in order to raise it again.
items.why: Students associate insulin with diabetes and with feeling faint from low blood sugar, and injections are given to make a person better, so they attach insulin to the low glucose situation instead of the high one. If the blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces the hormone insulin that causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is Type 1 diabetes normally treated?
items.correct: It is normally treated with insulin injections.
items.misconception: Type 1 diabetes is caused by eating too much sugar and is treated with a controlled diet and exercise.
items.why: Diet and exercise are heavily publicised as the answer to diabetes, and the two types are rarely separated in everyday reporting, so the treatment for Type 2 is applied to Type 1 as well. Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin and is normally treated with insulin injections; a carbohydrate controlled diet and an exercise regime are common treatments for Type 2 diabetes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does an intrauterine device do, and what does a spermicidal agent do?
items.correct: Intrauterine devices prevent the implantation of an embryo or release a hormone, and spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm.
items.misconception: Intrauterine devices work by killing sperm and spermicidal agents work by preventing an embryo implanting.
items.why: Both are non-hormonal methods learned in the same list, and neither is linked to a familiar picture of how it works, so the two mechanisms are attached to the wrong method. Intrauterine devices prevent the implantation of an embryo or release a hormone; spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How successful and how safe is IVF treatment?
items.correct: The success rates are not high, the treatment is very emotionally and physically stressful, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.
items.misconception: IVF nearly always works and carries no real risk to the mother or the babies.
items.why: IVF is reported through the successful births that make the news, and multiple births are presented as happy outcomes, so the failure rate and the risks are rarely part of the story students hear. Although fertility treatment gives a woman the chance to have a baby of her own, it is very emotionally and physically stressful, the success rates are not high, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What effect does thyroxine have on the basal metabolic rate?
items.correct: Thyroxine stimulates the basal metabolic rate.
items.misconception: Thyroxine lowers the basal metabolic rate, slowing the body's reactions down.
items.why: Thyroxine is introduced through negative feedback, where the language is all about reducing and inhibiting, so students attach the idea of lowering to the hormone itself rather than to the control of its level. Thyroxine from the thyroid gland stimulates the basal metabolic rate and plays an important role in growth and development; it is the release of thyroxine that is reduced when its level in the blood is too high.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
